newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed meets Tuesday to consider rate rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed meets Tuesday to consider rate rise.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve is scheduled to hold a pivotal meeting Tuesday to consider raising interest rates for the first time in about 1-1/2 years.

At issue is whether the U.S. economy is robust enough to reignite inflation -- which would call for a rate hike to keep prices in check -- or whether a rate increase would instead stifle a struggling economy.

A majority of economists polled by Reuters last week -- 17 of 30 -- believes the central bank will opt to raise short-term rates Tuesday, with all but one of those analysts expecting an increase of 0.25 percent.

Even a small rate hike would lead to higher borrowing costs for consumers and corporations, putting a damper on Wall Street and Main Street. President Bill Clinton, too, would balk at any brakes on the economy that would reduce his chances of a victory in the Nov. 5 election.

Conflicting signs about the economy's health present strong arguments for both camps in the Fed -- the anti-inflation hawks, mainly at the Fed's regional banks, and the so-called doves, mostly political appointees on the Fed board in Washington.
At a seven-year low of 5.1 percent, the unemployment rate is at a level that has historically led to higher inflation and demands for higher wages.
Wages, in fact, have already begun to pick up. But so far companies have been unable to pass through those higher labour costs to consumers in the form of price increases.

Firms have enjoyed fat profit margins for 5-1/2 years of economic expansion and thus have some leeway to absorb the higher labour costs. But it is not clear how long they can go without raising prices.
While the job market is tight, and companies are stepping up production and rebuilding inventories, retail sales have slowed and the housing market has weakened.

If the Fed tightens credit because wages are rising, it risks giving ammunition to critics who see it as a pawn of Wall Street. And if the Democrats then regain control of Congress, lawmakers may seize on the pre-election rate rise as a reason to rein in the Fed, especially the regional banks.

On the other hand, some of Clinton's appointees to the Fed board may be sensitive to suspicions that they would favour the president and thus be more inclined to raise rates to prove their mettle to the markets and their colleagues.
Eight of the 12 regional Fed banks have called for a rate increase, and consensus-minded central bank Chairman Alan Greenspan may give in to avoid a revolt Tuesday.

In the end, the Fed's decision may be more important symbolically than economically. While a small rate rise would have only a minor impact on the economy and could easily be reversed later, it would clearly signal the Fed's priorities, and that is why Wall Street and Washington are watching so closely.
